demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette:
**Vignette: Fatima, Age 75**

Fatima has spent the better part of four decades on the bench. She is a woman who built her career on the belief that reason and order can be imposed upon chaos — that facts can be weighed, that verdicts can be reached, that the world yields to careful deliberation. She carried that belief into every corner of her life. It served her well, until the morning eighteen months ago when her youngest son, Tariq, died without warning.

He was forty-four years old. He had kissed his wife goodbye, driven to work, and collapsed in the parking garage of his office building from a cardiac arrest that no one had seen coming. There had been no illness, no warning, no opportunity for Fatima to prepare herself. Her daughter-in-law called her directly, and Fatima remembers standing in her kitchen holding the phone, watching the coffee she had just poured send a thin curl of steam into the air, unable to understand why something so ordinary was still happening while her son was gone.

She flew to be with the family within hours. She managed the arrangements with the composure people expected of her. She received mourners, she recited prayers, she held her grandchildren. Her husband, Samir, wept openly. Fatima did not — not then, and not for weeks afterward. She told herself she was being strong. She returned to the courtroom within ten days.

What she did not tell anyone was that she had stopped sleeping. She lies awake most nights beside Samir, replaying the phone call, or imagining Tariq alone on the cold concrete of that parking garage. She constructs alternative timelines obsessively — if she had called him that morning as she almost did, if he had been running late, if someone had found him sooner. The thoughts arrive uninvited and will not be reasoned away, which unsettles her deeply. She is a woman who has always been able to reason things away.

On the bench, she finds herself distracted in ways she has never experienced before. She loses the thread of testimony. She catches herself staring at a young male attorney who has Tariq's particular way of tilting his head when he is thinking, and she has to grip the edge of her desk beneath the bench to anchor herself. She has not told her clerk, who has worked with her for eleven years, that anything is wrong. She is a judge. She does not come apart in public.

At home, the distance between what she shows and what she feels has grown into something exhausting. She avoids the guest room where Tariq used to sleep when he visited. She has asked Samir not to play the particular style of Arabic music Tariq loved, and when Samir forgot one evening and put it on, she left the room without explanation and sat alone in the garden until it was dark. She does not want to hurt Samir, but she cannot explain the way certain things seem to reach inside her chest and pull.

She describes herself as feeling hollowed out — present in her body, going through the motions of a life that looks intact from the outside, but inwardly disconnected from almost everything that once gave her pleasure. She used to love hosting family dinners. She used to enjoy the theater. She used to feel pride when she put on her robe each morning. Now the robe feels like a costume.

What brought her, finally, to seek help was a moment in her courtroom three weeks ago. A young man was being sentenced, and his mother in the gallery began to cry — a quiet, helpless sound — and Fatima had to call a recess. She sat alone in her chambers for twenty minutes, shaking, before she could return. She had never called an unnecessary recess in her life. It frightened her more than anything else had.

She comes to sessions composed and precise, choosing her words with the care of someone who has spent a lifetime weighing language. But beneath that composure, she is a mother who cannot find a place to put her grief.
